Lebesgue measure of distance sets with regular pins and multi-scale Mizohata-Takeuchi-type estimatesThanks: This work is supported by the National Key R&D Program of China 2024YFA1015400, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China grant 12131011.

Bochen Liu Email address: Bochen.Liu1989@gmail.com Address: Department of Mathematics & International Center for Mathematics, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China
Abstract.

Suppose E,FE,F are Borel sets in the plane, dimℋE>1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E>1, dimℋE+dimℋF>2\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E+\dim_{\mathcal{H}}F>2, and FF has equal Hausdorff and packing dimension. We prove that there exists y∈Fy\in F such that the pinned distance set

Δy​(E):={|x−y|:x∈E}\Delta_{y}(E):=\{|x-y|:x\in E\}

has positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, it settles the regular case of the distance set problem in the plane. The main ingredients of the proof consist of a multi-scale Good-Bad decomposition and a multi-scale Mizohata-Takeuchi-type estimate with arbitrary small power-loss.

1. Introduction

1.1. Falconer distance conjecture

Falconer distance conjecture [17] is one of the most famous open problems in harmonic analysis and geometric measure theory since 1985. It states that, if a Borel set E⊂ℝdE\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, d⩾2d\geqslant 2, has Hausdorff dimension dimℋE>d/2\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E>d/2, then its distance set

Δ(E):={|x−y|:x,y∈E}\Delta(E):=\{|x-y|:x,y\in E\}

has positive Lebesgue measure (denoted by |Δ⁡(E)|>0|\Delta(E)|>0). A stronger version is the pinned distance set problem, first studied by Peres and Schlag [40] in 2000, that asks whether there exists y∈Ey\in E such that the pinned distance set

Δy​(E):={|x−y|:x∈E}\Delta_{y}(E):=\{|x-y|:x\in E\}

has positive Lebesgue measure when dimℋE>d/2\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E>d/2.

With more than 40 years passed, accumulating efforts of many excellent mathematicians, Falconer distance conjecture is still open in every dimension. So far, there are two perspectives to study this problem. One is to investigate how large dimℋE\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E needs to be to ensure Δ⁡(E)\Delta(E) or Δy​(E)\Delta_{y}(E) has positive Lebesgue measure. Falconer’s first result [17] in 1985 is of this type, which is a L∞L^{\infty}-estimate in today’s point of view. In 1987, Mattila [34] proposed his L2L^{2}-approach for |Δ⁡(E)||\Delta(E)|, now called the Mattila integral, that reduced the problem to spherical averaging operators. Since then, Bourgain [3], Wolff [48], Erdogan [16], Du-Guth-Ou-Wang-Wilson-Zhang [11], Du-Zhang [15] have used the newly developed tools in harmonic analysis at the time to improve spherical averaging estimates for partial results on Falconer distance conjecture.

In 2019, the author [31] proposed an L2L^{2}-approach for the pinned distance set problem. Shortly after, Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang [26] proved the current best-known result on Falconer distance conjecture in the plane:

dimℋE>5/4⟹|Δy​(E)|>0, for some ​y∈E,\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E>5/4\implies|\Delta_{y}(E)|>0,\text{ for some }y\in E,

building on the author’s approach and an insightful use of the decoupling theory. Their argument in fact shows

dimℋF>1, 3​dimℋE+dimℋF>5⟹|Δy​(E)|>0, for some ​y∈F.\dim_{\mathcal{H}}F>1,\ 3\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E+\dim_{\mathcal{H}}F>5\implies|\Delta_{y}(E)|>0,\text{ for some }y\in F.

We shall review their proof strategy in Section 3.1. This result was later extended to all even dimensions by Du-Iosevich-Ou-Wang-Zhang [12]. Following the same idea with more careful analysis, Du-Ou-Ren-Zhang [13][14] obtained the current best-known results in dimension 33 and higher.

The other perspective on Falconer distance conjecture is to compute the Hausdorff dimension of Δ​(E),Δy​(E)\Delta(E),\Delta_{y}(E) assuming dimℋE>d/2\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E>d/2. The first nontrivial result on Δ⁡(E)\Delta(E) is due to Katz-Tao [29] and Bourgain [4] from discretized sum-product estimates. Its pinned version is due to Shmerkin [42]. The first nontrivial explicit dimensional exponent is due to Keleti and Shmerkin [30], who proposed the novel idea of scale-selection. A partial result based on estimates of Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang was given by the author [32], that was later extended to all even dimensions by Wang-Zheng [47].

The current record in the plane is due to Stull [46], who proved

dimℋE>1⟹dimℋΔy​(E)⩾34, for some ​y∈E.\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E>1\implies\dim_{\mathcal{H}}\Delta_{y}(E)\geqslant\frac{3}{4},\text{ for some }y\in E.

His method is beyond the author’s understanding (as well as the recent work of Fiedler-Stull [20][21]), but according to Hong Wang (personal communication), she and Shmerkin understand the key idea of Stull [46] and are able to obtain the same dimensional exponent 34\frac{3}{4} via incidence estimates. We also refer to the recent work of Shmerkin and Wang [41] for partial results on the endpoint case dimℋE⩾d/2\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E\geqslant d/2 for all d⩾2d\geqslant 2.

Recently, the less well-known Assouad dimension dimA\dim_{A} has drawn much attention. The problem on dimAΔ⁡(E)\dim_{A}\Delta(E) in terms of dimAE\dim_{A}E has been solved by Fraser in the plane [24][25]. There is also a very recent work of Fraser-Pham [22] on the relation between the Fourier dimension of EE and the Hausdorff dimension of Δ⁡(E)\Delta(E).

Though open in general, the distance set problem is better understood on sets with regularity. Bárány [2], Orponen [37] studied self-similar sets, Ferguson-Fraser-Sahlsten [19] studied self-affine sets, Fraser-Pollicott [23] studied self-conformal sets. A breakthrough in bypassing dynamical systems was Orponen’s work [38] on Ahlfors-David regular sets, and the idea was further developed by Shmerkin [43][44], Keleti-Shmerkin [30]. The final version can be stated as the following: suppose E,FE,F are Borel sets in the plane, then

dimℋF>1,dimℋE=dimPE>1⟹dimℋΔy​(E)=1, for some ​y∈E,\dim_{\mathcal{H}}F>1,\ \dim_{\mathcal{H}}E=\dim_{P}E>1\implies\dim_{\mathcal{H}}\Delta_{y}(E)=1,\text{ for some }y\in E,

where dimP\dim_{P} denotes the packing dimension (see Section 2 below for definition). In particular, if E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} has equal Hausdorff and packing dimension >1>1, then dimℋΔy​(E)=1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}\Delta_{y}(E)=1 for some y∈Ey\in E.

“dimℋΔ⁡(E)=1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}\Delta(E)=1” is exciting and already answers the original question of Falconer in [17], but it is still weaker than “positive Lebesgue measure”. There is very little discussion on Lebesgue measure of distance sets of regular sets in the literature. The only work we know is due to Iosevich and the author [28] on |Δ⁡(A1×A2)||\Delta(A_{1}\times A_{2})| with A1,A2⊂ℝA_{1},A_{2}\subset\mathbb{R}, Ahlfors-David regular, dimA1+dimA2>43−ϵ0\dim A_{1}+\dim A_{2}>\frac{4}{3}-\epsilon_{0}.

In this paper, we settle the regular case of the distance set problem in the plane.

Theorem 1.1.

Suppose E,FE,F are Borel sets in the plane, dimℋE>1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E>1, dimℋE+dimℋF>2\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E+\dim_{\mathcal{H}}F>2, and FF has equal Hausdorff and packing dimension. Then there exists y∈Fy\in F such that the pinned distance set

Δy​(E):={|x−y|:x∈E}\Delta_{y}(E):=\{|x-y|:x\in E\}

has positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, if E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} has equal Hausdorff and packing dimension >1>1, then |Δy​(E)|>0|\Delta_{y}(E)|>0 for some y∈Ey\in E.

Notice that there exists E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}, dimℋE=dimPE=1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E=\dim_{P}E=1, while |Δ⁡(E)|=0|\Delta(E)|=0. For example, one can take E=A×{0}E=A\times\{0\} with

A:=⋂i=1∞{a∈[0,1]:dist⁡(a,qi−1​ℤ)<qi−1−ϵi},A:=\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty}\{a\in[0,1]:\operatorname{dist}(a,q_{i}^{-1}\mathbb{Z})<q_{i}^{-1-\epsilon_{i}}\},

where qi+1>qii>1q_{i+1}>q_{i}^{i}>1 and ϵi↓0\epsilon_{i}\downarrow 0 such that 10​qi−ϵi→010q_{i}^{-\epsilon_{i}}\rightarrow 0. Then dimℋA=dimPA=1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}A=\dim_{P}A=1 (see, for example, Section 8.5 in [18] for dimℋA⩾1−ϵi\dim_{\mathcal{H}}A\geqslant 1-\epsilon_{i}, ∀i\forall\,i, and it is well known that dimℋA⩽dimPA⩽1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}A\leqslant\dim_{P}A\leqslant 1). Therefore dimℋE=dimPE=1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E=\dim_{P}E=1, while

|Δ⁡(E)|=|A−A|⩽10​qi−ϵi→0.|\Delta(E)|=|A-A|\leqslant 10q_{i}^{-\epsilon_{i}}\rightarrow 0.

The main ingredients of the proof of Theorem 1.1 consist of a multi-scale Good-Bad decomposition and a multi-scale Mizohata-Takeuchi-type estimate with arbitrary small power-loss. The single-scale Good-Bad decomposition was proposed by Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang [26]. Our multi-scale Good-Bad decomposition is inspired by them, but not a direct generalization (see the discussion in Section 3.2). As a result of the difference, it is the first time in recent works that dimℋF⩽1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}F\leqslant 1 is allowed for |Δy​(E)|>0|\Delta_{y}(E)|>0 or dimΔy​(E)=1\dim\Delta_{y}(E)=1, y∈Fy\in F. Also, unlike the refined decoupling inequality in [26], there is no deep LpL^{p} theory in this paper. We develop an L2L^{2} ball inflation argument that has its own interest (see Section 4). It also leaves plenty of room for more tools to play a role in this framework.

1.2. Mizohata-Takeuchi conjecture

Let Σ\Sigma be a compact C2C^{2} hypersurface in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with surface measure σ\sigma. The Mizohata-Takeuchi conjecture arose in the study of dispersive PDE from 1970s. It states that, for every non-negative weight ww on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

∫ℝd|f​d​σ^​(x)|2​w​(x)​𝑑x≲supTw⁡(T)​∫Σ|f|2​𝑑σ,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\widehat{f\,d\sigma}(x)|^{2}w(x)dx\lesssim\sup_{T}w(T)\int_{\Sigma}|f|^{2}d\sigma,

where w⁡(T):=∫Tww(T):=\int_{T}w and the supremum is taken over all 1-neighborhoods of doubly-infinite lines. When Σ\Sigma is a hyperplane, it simply follows from Plancherel. On the other hand, unfortunately, it has been proved false on every hypersurface that is not part of a hyperplane, by a recent delicate example of Cairo [6]. For more information on the history, related works, and discussion on the Mizohata-Takeuchi conjecture, we refer to the inspiring talk of Guth [27], comprehensive introductions of Carbery-Iliopoulou-Wang [8], Cairo [6], Cairo-Zhang [5], as well as recent works of Carbery-Hänninen-Valdimarsson [7], Carbery-Li-Pang-Yung [9], Mulherkar [36], and references therein.

One way to describe how far it is from being true is to consider its local version:

∫BR|f​d​σ^​(x)|2​w​(x)​𝑑x⩽C​Rα⋅supTw⁡(T)​∫Σ|f|2​𝑑σ.\int_{B_{R}}|\widehat{f\,d\sigma}(x)|^{2}w(x)dx\leqslant CR^{\alpha}\cdot\sup_{T}w(T)\int_{\Sigma}|f|^{2}d\sigma. (1.1)

Though the original Mizohata-Takeuchi conjecture fails in general, it is an open problem that whether (1.1) holds for every α>0\alpha>0, called the local Mizohata-Takeuchi conjecture. In [8], Carbery, Iliopoulou and Wang proved (1.1) for every α>d−1d+1\alpha>\frac{d-1}{d+1} on strictly convex C2C^{2} hypersurfaces. Whether d−1d+1\frac{d-1}{d+1} is optimal is not known, but Guth [27] pointed out that a Rd−1d+1−ϵR^{\frac{d-1}{d+1}-\epsilon}-power-loss is inevitable under the usual “wave packet decomposition axioms”. See [8] for a detailed discussion on Guth’s outline.

In a very recent work of Cairo-Zhang [5], a family of counterexamples are constructed, that in particular shows the exponent of Carbery-Iliopoulou-Wang is sharp for many strictly convex C2C^{2} hypersurfaces up to the endpoint. But whether it is sharp for specific surfaces, even for familiar ones like the paraboloid or the sphere, is still unknown.

We call (1.1) “single-scale” as all tubes under consideration have the same size. In this paper, we find that some multi-scale Mizohata-Takeuchi-type estimates have no power-loss, up to an arbitrary small constant δ>0\delta>0. The one we need for Theorem 1.1 is quite complicated to state. Instead, we state the following baby version in the introduction. This observation is also where this project started.

From now we only consider the case Σ=Sd−1\Sigma=S^{d-1}, because our motivation is on the distance set problem. The proof also works on more general surfaces for associated results.

Proposition 1.2.

Let σ\sigma denote the surface measure on Sd−1S^{d-1}. Suppose ww is a non-negative weight on BR⊂ℝdB_{R}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, 0<δ≪1/20<\delta\ll 1/2 is a constant, and

Rδ=r0<⋯<rM=RR^{\delta}=r_{0}<\cdots<r_{M}=R

is a sequence with rj+1⩽rj2r_{j+1}\leqslant r_{j}^{2}. Then

w(BR)−1∫BR|f​d​σ^|2w≲d,δ,MRC​δ(∏j=0M−1sup∀Qj+1∈𝒟rj+1∀Tj∈𝕋rj,rj+1wQj+1(Tj))∥f∥L2​(Sd−1)2,w(B_{R})^{-1}\int_{B_{R}}|\widehat{f\,d\sigma}|^{2}w\lesssim_{d,\delta,M}R^{C\delta}\left(\prod_{j=0}^{M-1}\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\forall\,Q_{j+1}\in\mathcal{D}_{r_{j+1}}\\ \forall\,T_{j}\in\mathbb{T}_{r_{j},r_{j+1}}\end{subarray}}w_{Q_{j+1}}(T_{j})\right)\|f\|_{L^{2}(S^{d-1})}^{2},

where 𝒟rj+1\mathcal{D}_{r_{j+1}} denotes the collection of almost disjoint rj+1r_{j+1}-cubes, 𝕋rj,rj+1\mathbb{T}_{r_{j},r_{j+1}} denotes the collection of rj×⋯×rj×rj+1r_{j}\times\cdots\times r_{j}\times r_{j+1} tubes, w⁡(BR):=∫BRww(B_{R}):=\int_{B_{R}}w, wQ​(T):=w​(Q)−1​∫T∩Qww_{Q}(T):=w(Q)^{-1}\int_{T\cap Q}w, and C>0C>0 is a constant independent in R,M,δR,M,\delta.

When w=χBRw=\chi_{B_{R}}, this result becomes

∥f​d​σ^∥L2​(BR)2≲d,δRC​δ⋅R∥f∥L2​(Sd−1)2,\|\widehat{f\,d\sigma}\|_{L^{2}(B_{R})}^{2}\lesssim_{d,\delta}R^{C\delta}\cdot R\|f\|_{L^{2}(S^{d-1})}^{2},

which coincides with the classical sharp estimate of Agmon-Hörmander [1] up to a factor RC​δR^{C\delta}. The constrain rj+1⩽rj2r_{j+1}\leqslant r_{j}^{2} in Proposition 1.2 is due to technical reasons. This is also why we need some regularity on the pin set FF in Theorem 1.1. I wonder if it is necessary.

A heuristic proof of Proposition 1.2 is given in Section 4.1 to illustrate the idea of our L2L^{2} ball inflation. A detailed discussion on the version for Theorem 1.1 is given in Section 4.2.

Organization

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review different dimensions and some standard techniques in modern harmonic analysis. In Section 3, we first review the single-scale Good-Bad decomposition of Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang, then introduce our multi-scale Good-Bad decomposition and prove the L1L^{1}-estimate of our bad part. In Section 4, we first give a heuristic proof of Proposition 1.2, then give a detailed proof of the L2L^{2}-estimate of our good part. In Section 5, we use our estimates on good and bad parts to prove Theorem 1.1.

2. Preliminaries

Let ℳ⁡(E)\mathcal{M}(E) denote the family of finite Borel measures supported on a compact subset of EE. There are two equivalent ways to define Hausdorff dimension of sets E⊂ℝdE\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} in terms of measures:

dimℋE\displaystyle\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E =sups{s:∃μ∈ℳ(E) with μ(B(x,r))<rs,∀x∈ℝd,r>0}\displaystyle=\sup_{s}\{s:\exists\,\mu\in\mathcal{M}(E)\text{ with }\mu(B(x,r))<r^{s},\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},r>0\}
=sups{s:∃μ∈ℳ⁡(E)​ with ​Is​(μ)<∞},\displaystyle=\sup_{s}\{s:\exists\,\mu\in\mathcal{M}(E)\text{ with }I_{s}(\mu)<\infty\},

where Is​(μ)I_{s}(\mu) is the ss-dimension energy of μ\mu defined by

Is​(μ):=∬|x−y|−s​𝑑μ​(x)​𝑑μ​(y)=cs,d​∫|μ^​(ξ)|2​|ξ|−d+s​𝑑ξ.I_{s}(\mu):=\iint|x-y|^{-s}d\mu(x)d\mu(y)=c_{s,d}\int|\widehat{\mu}(\xi)|^{2}|\xi|^{-d+s}d\xi.

A finite Borel measure μ\mu satisfying

μ⁡(B⁡(x,r))≲rs,∀x∈ℝd,r>0,\mu(B(x,r))\lesssim r^{s},\,\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},r>0,

is called a Frostman measure of dimension ss.

Let N⁡(E,r)N(E,r) denote the smallest number of rr-balls needed to cover EE. The upper Minkowski dimension (also called the upper box-counting dimension) is defined by

dim¯M​E:=lim supr→0log⁡N⁡(E,r)log⁡1/r.\overline{\dim}_{M}E:=\limsup_{r\rightarrow 0}\frac{\log N(E,r)}{\log 1/r}.

The packing dimension of EE, denoted by dimPE\dim_{P}E, is defined by

dimPE:=inf{supidim¯MEi:E=⋃i=1∞Ei,Ei is bounded}.\dim_{P}E:=\inf\{\sup_{i}\overline{\dim}_{M}E_{i}:E=\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}E_{i},E_{i}\text{ is bounded}\}.

In particular, for every finite Borel measure μ\mu on EE and every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists Ei⊂EE_{i}\subset E such that dim¯M​Ei<dimPE+ϵ\overline{\dim}_{M}E_{i}<\dim_{P}E+\epsilon and μ⁡(Ei)>0\mu(E_{i})>0.

It is easy to verify that dimℋE⩽dimPE⩽dim¯M​E\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E\leqslant\dim_{P}E\leqslant\overline{\dim}_{M}E, and dimℋE=dimPE\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E=\dim_{P}E if EE is Ahlfors-David regular (not vice versa). For details and more discussion on their relations, we refer to Mattila’s books [35] as a reference.

We will need several standard techniques in modern harmonic analysis. We only state the version for our use. The proofs are not hard, so we omit details and refer to, for example, Guth’s lecture notes (see his homepage) as a reference.

3. A multi-scale Good-Bad decomposition

3.1. The single-scale Good-Bad decomposition of Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang

For nearly 30 years, the L2L^{2}-method has been the most efficient approach to the Falconer distance conjecture, until Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang [26] pointed out that it cannot beat Wolff’s partial result in the plane [48]. To go further, they proposed the novel Good-Bad decomposition as follows.

Let R0R_{0} be a large dyadic number and Ri:=2i​R0R_{i}:=2^{i}R_{0}. 1=ψ0+∑i⩾1∑θ:Ri−1/2-capsψi,θ.1=\psi_{0}+\sum_{i\geqslant 1}\sum_{\theta:\,R_{i}^{-1/2}\text{-caps}}\psi_{i,\theta}. (3.1)

3.2. A multi-scale Good-Bad decomposition

We call the Good-Bad decomposition of Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang “single-scale”, as only Ri−1/2+δ×1R_{i}^{-1/2+\delta}\times 1 tubes are considered for each i⩾1i\geqslant 1.

In this paper, we propose a multi-scale Good-Bad decomposition. Though inspired by Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang, our Good-Bad decomposition is not a direct generalization of theirs. Heavy tubes are removed in different ways. In [26], Orponen’s LpL^{p} radial projection estimate (3.6) is used to remove heavy tubes on FF, while in this paper, it is used to remove heavy tubes on EE, then an L2L^{2}-technique removes heavy tubes on FF. See the proof of Proposition 3.3 below for details. This is also why dimℋF⩽1\dim_{\mathcal{H}}F\leqslant 1 is allowed in our Theorem 1.1.

∫|μg​o​o​d,i,Q⁡(y)∗σR^​(y)|2​𝑑ν​(y)≲∫|((μg​o​o​d,i,Q⁡(y)^​d​σR)∗ψ)∨​(y)|2​𝑑ν​(y),\int|\mu_{good,i,Q(y)}*\widehat{\sigma_{R}}(y)|^{2}d\nu(y)\lesssim\int|((\widehat{\mu_{good,i,Q(y)}}d\sigma_{R})*\psi)^{\vee}(y)|^{2}d\nu(y), (4.3)

5. Proof of the main Theorem

Now we can prove Theorem 1.1. By the discussion in Section 2, there exist a probability measure μ\mu on EE of finite ss-energy Is​(μ)I_{s}(\mu) for some s>1s>1, and a probability measure ν\nu on FF that is Frostman of dimension t>2−st>2-s with dim¯M​supp⁡ν<t+δ2\overline{\dim}_{M}\operatorname{supp}\nu<t+\delta^{2}. Then, by Proposition 3.2, Proposition 4.1, and

1=\displaystyle 1= ∫(∫Δy​(E)d∗y​(μ))​dν​(y)\displaystyle\int\left(\int_{\Delta_{y}(E)}d^{y}_{*}(\mu)\right)d\nu(y)
⩽\displaystyle\leqslant ∥d∗y(μg​o​o​d,y)−d∗y(μ))∥L1+(supy∈supp⁡ν|Δy(E)|12)∥d∗y(μg​o​o​d,y)∥L2,\displaystyle\|d_{*}^{y}(\mu_{good,y})-d_{*}^{y}(\mu))\|_{L^{1}}+(\sup_{y\in\operatorname{supp}\nu}|\Delta_{y}(E)|^{\frac{1}{2}})\|d_{*}^{y}(\mu_{good,y})\|_{L^{2}},

one can conclude that

|Δy​(E)|>0,for some ​y∈F,|\Delta_{y}(E)|>0,\ \text{for some }y\in F,

that completes the proof of Theorem 1.1.
